sources.title: NPR Topics: Home Page Top Stories

articles.author: Liz Ruskin
articles.description: Former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola has narrowly won Alaska's U.S. Senate race, toppling the Republican incumbent, according to a race call by The Associated Press.
articles.title: Mary Peltola flips Alaska's Senate seat into Democrats' column

articles.author: Joel Rose
articles.description: On the heels of an air traffic meltdown, families of the 67 killed in a mid-air crash near Reagan National Airport call on lawmakers to pass an aviation safety bill.
articles.title: Families push more air safety measures as FAA grapples with system improvements

articles.author: Michelle Aslam
articles.description: NPR's Sacha Pfeiffer speaks with cybersecurity expert Dmitri Alperovitch about the coincidence of several major technical failures in IT infrastructure — and how best to understand it.
articles.title: Air travel, Microsoft, banking: Why are our IT systems failing?

articles.author: Tonya Mosley
articles.description: The longtime host of Reading Rainbow is telling his own story. Burton opened a window to the past in Roots and helped imagine a different future on Star Trek. His new memoir is Take My Word for It.
articles.title: Take a look, it's in his book: LeVar Burton writes a memoir

articles.author: The Associated Press
articles.description: Iran fired drones on Tuesday at a U.S. radar facility in Bahrain, and the U.S. retaliated by firing at Iranian targets along an important shipping route.
articles.title: Iran launches a third round of strikes on Bahrain, host of U.S. Navy's 5th Fleet

articles.author: Shannon Bond
articles.description: The former Nvidia CEO said he would be "honored" to return if the board allowed. But the board says it has no intention of reinstating him.
articles.title: Nvidia board says it does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO

articles.author: Michel Martin
articles.description: Sen. Jack Reed raised concerns about FAA oversight of contractors after last week's nationwide ground stop and criticized the Trump administration's request for $50 billion in additional funding.
articles.title: Sen. Jack Reed says FAA needs a real plan, not just more money

articles.author: Greg Rosalsky
articles.description: In late October, Google had the worst stock day in its history as a public company. The Planet Money newsletter asks: has Google been caught in "the innovator's dilemma"?
articles.title: Can Google win the AI race without killing its cash cow?

articles.author: Mara Gordon
articles.description: Has your doctor asked whether they can use artificial intelligence to take notes during an exam? It's very popular, and here's how to think through the pros and the cons of the new technology.
articles.title: I'm a human doctor with human intelligence. But I sure do like my AI notetaker

articles.author: The Associated Press
articles.description: Manila is President Trump's first stop on a three-day trip that will later take him to China for historic three-way nuclear talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
articles.title: Trump arrives in Philippines to kick off Asia trip

articles.author: Australian Associated Press
articles.description:
Royal commission sees text message where Bandidos member Joel Leavitt says ‘just make up a quote that hits 20K’ while working on site for CFMEU

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A Bandidos gang member says it is possible he used a fake $20,000 invoice for souvlaki to pocket thousands of dollars while employed on a Big Build site.
The former CFMEU member and bikie Joel Leavitt faced a second day of examination by the royal commission into alleged corruption across Victoria’s construction sector on Wednesday.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Bikie ‘not surprised’ if he used fake $20,000 souvlaki invoice to pocket thousands on Big Build site, inquiry hears

articles.author: Kate Lamb
articles.description:
Summit in Chinese tech hub Shenzhen set to include highly anticipated meeting between Xi, Trump and Putin

Shenzhen takes centre stage as Xi sends ‘Chinamaxxing’ message at Apec summit

What is Apec? Explained in 30 seconds

Yalta became a byword for betrayal. Will Trump, Xi and Putin enact another carve-up?
That is the question the Guardian’s diplomatic correspondent Patrick Wintour seeks to address in his piece about the expected, Putin, Trump and Xi, meeting at Apec on Thursday.
It is a truism in diplomacy that if you are not around the table, the risk is that you, or your values, are on the menu and about to be carved up. Many excluded from the summit in Shenzhen, principally Ukraine but also eastern Europe and Baltic countries, Taiwan and even Iran, have reason to be nervous that their sponsors might abandon them in a complex geopolitical trade-off that Putin envisions, and Trump seems to endorse.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Apec summit live: Xi and Putin start talks; Rubio says Trump serious about meeting Kim Jong-un

articles.author: Associated Press
articles.description:
The US secretary of state was speaking after Microsoft, major banks, and the National Security Agency were all affected by technical failures in recent days
US secretary of state Marco Rubio has sought to assure Americans that there’s “zero” information that the cascade of service outages – which have grounded flights, cut off work access, limited bank access and disrupted classified communications – are related to each other or to a malign actor.
In recent days, Microsoft, major US banks, American air traffic control systems and the National Security Agency have all been affected by technical failures and outages. Donald Trump has faced a groundswell of criticism as friends and foes alike demand the White House answer for the disruptions.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Zero’ evidence that recent cascade of tech outages are linked, says Rubio

articles.author: Andrew Gregory Health editor
articles.description:
Campaign groups and regulators say data breaches are distressing for patients and families and erode trust in the health service
The NHS in England has recorded more than 3,000 incidents of staff inappropriately snooping on patients’ medical records in the last five years.
Patient campaign groups and regulators said the figures were “deeply concerning” and distressing for patients and families, and eroded trust in the health service. A lack of transparency from NHS organisations after data breaches were uncovered further compounded the heartache, they added.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Deeply concerning’: NHS in England reports more than 3,000 incidents of staff snooping on patients’ records

articles.author: Robyn Vinter North of England correspondent
articles.description:
Lasting cross-class friendships involve routinely ‘taking the piss’ out of the more privileged party, research by the LSE shows
Routinely “taking the piss” out of more privileged friends is one of the main ways people cope with a class difference in their friendships, research has found.
Cross-class friendships are widespread and mutually beneficial, a study by the London School of Economics showed, but a class gap can still pose an “omnipresent threat” to friendships.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: How to deal with a class difference in friendships? Make fun of your privileged friends

articles.author: Krishani Dhanji and Sarah Basford Canales
articles.description:
Amid widespread condemnation of the proposal, Pauline Hanson also wants to scrap existing parent and aged parent visa program

Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

One Nation has vowed to cut Australia’s refugee intake by 90% and scrap the permanent parent visa program under its latest hardline plan to slash migration.
Pauline Hanson announced the policy on Tuesday, labelling it a “tough” approach to migration. It was quickly criticised by political opponents and advocacy groups who labelled the announcement a “predictable and cheap” attack on refugees.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Devastating consequences’: One Nation plan to slash Australia’s refugee program denounced

articles.author: Dan Milmo Global technology editor
articles.description:
Meaning and use of word has become more important in age of AI chatbot, says dictionary
In a world where the line between people and machines is more blurred than ever, Cambridge dictionary has sided with natural intelligence for its word of the year: human.
Breakthroughs in artificial intelligence – led by the arrival of ChatGPT three years ago – have made the question of what it means to be human as vexed as ever, but the dictionary has drawn a firm line with its choice of the word of 2026, defining “human” as “having the qualities, faults, and feelings that people have, as opposed to gods, animals, or machines”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Human’ wins Cambridge dictionary’s word of the year

articles.author: Jennifer Rankin in Brussels
articles.description:
Leaked documents raise questions about claims Egypt met welfare targets to qualify for €2.5bn in loans
The European Commission has been accused of sugarcoating figures to enable it to release funds to Egypt under a landmark pact with the authoritarian government of Abdel Fatah al-Sisi.
The charge relates to a €7.4bn deal promised by Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, to al-Sisi on a high-profile visit to Cairo in 2024. The three-year “strategic and comprehensive partnership” was intended to bolster Egypt’s shaky economy, deter migrants from coming to Europe and shore up a region reeling from the 7 October attacks and Israel’s war on Gaza.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: European Commission accused of sugarcoating figures to release funds to Egypt

articles.author: Hanad Ahmed
articles.description:
Research also shows consuming wine could cut risk, reopening debate on whether beverage has health benefits
Drinking beer and spirits increases the risk of serious kidney damage, whereas consuming wine offers protection against it, a study suggests.
People who drink nine units of spirits a week are 26% more likely to suffer acute kidney injury than those who consume only one unit a week.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Drinking beer and spirits raises risk of acute kidney damage, study suggests

articles.author: Patrick Commins Economics editor
articles.description:
Wage rates climb about 1 percentage point faster than before pandemic, triggering warnings of a sixth RBA rate rise

Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

Wages grew at their fastest pace since late 2023 over the three months to September, buoyed up by this year’s boost to minimum pay rates for millions of lower paid workers – but still not fast enough to keep up with the rising cost of living.
The Australian Bureau of Statistics’ wage price index climbed by 1.1% in the most recent quarter, lifting the annual increase to 3.5% – a pace that economists said would keep the Reserve Bank on edge about the need for further interest rate hikes.
Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Australian wages grow at fastest pace since 2023 – but prices are climbing even more quickly

articles.author: Ed Pilkington in Anchorage, Alaska
articles.description:
Peltola, the first Alaska Native in the US Senate, ran a campaign that drew universal issues from her own Indigenous politics
Late into the night on 3 November, while the lower 48 states were reeling from the blue wave crashing across the US, Mary Peltola took to the stage in a Sheraton Hotel ballroom in Anchorage, Alaska, to greet her supporters.
It wasn’t a victory speech as such – there would still be long days ahead before all votes could be counted across this vast arctic state. But that didn’t prevent the Democratic Senate candidate from expressing her elation, bouncing up and down on stage, clapping her hands and clicking her fingers.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Aarigaa!’: the triumph of Mary Peltola’s historic US Senate win and what it means for Alaska Natives

articles.author: Cait Kelly
articles.description:
Law reform body recommends ongoing ban on commercial surrogacy, but greater compensation for surrogates, and safeguards around who the child’s legal parents are

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Surrogates would be entitled to full compensation, with a nationally consistent framework ensuring domestic surrogacy is a viable option to parenthood, under proposed changes by Australia’s law reform body.
The Australian Law Reform Commission has been investigating how to better regulate surrogacy and harmonise laws so they are consistent with international legal obligations, while protecting human rights – particularly the rights and best interests of the child.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Australia’s ‘problematic’ surrogacy laws could be transformed under proposed changes

articles.author: Chris Stein
articles.description:
Republican incumbent beaten in race dominated by controversy over second candidate named Dan Sullivan
Democrat Mary Peltola will be Alaska’s next senator after beating the Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan, with the result called two weeks on from midterm elections which saw Donald Trump’s party lose ground across the country.
Peltola, a former US House lawmaker, is the first Democrat the state has elected to the Senate since 2008. Her victory comes just two years after Alaska voters unseated her while supporting Trump by a double-digit margin.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Mary Peltola beats Republican Dan Sullivan in Alaska to give Democrats 56 Senate seats

articles.author: Cecilia Nowell, Shrai Popat, Lucy Campbell and Tom Ambrose
articles.description:
This live blog is now closed.

White House withdraws nomination of Heidi Overton to lead FDA

Sign up for US Breaking News email

Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic-Senator elect from Michigan, said today that he would be happy to work with the Trump administration to pass one of his tentpole policy agenda items – Medicare For All.
“Everybody’s like, ‘ah well, you’d work with Donald Trump to get Medicare For All?’. I’m like hell yeah, because the point for me is Medicare For All. I don’t care who puts their name on it. I need to go back and talk to Michiganders, and I need to know that our service made their lives easier,” he said at the Atlantic Summit in Washington DC.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: White House pulls nomination of Heidi Overton to lead Food and Drug Administration – as it happened

articles.author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
articles.description:
Phenomenon is not a common occurrence in the Bay area and inclement weather is expected to continue for few days
A pair of waterspouts were recorded recently in the San Francisco Bay area, much to the delight and shock of several observers, as storms pummelled the region.
Two waterspouts – vortexes of air and water mist, essentially tornadoes – cut a sheer streak into the sky, as they spiraled above the bay, according to social media footage capturing the weather phenomenon.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Tag team: dual waterspouts appear in San Francisco Bay amid stormy weather

articles.author: Nick Visser
articles.description:
After a 13-year wait for the latest Grand Theft Auto instalment, Thursday’s launch is shaping up to be ‘the biggest gaming event that’s ever been’
Gamers across Australia are preparing for the once-in-a-generation release of Grand Theft Auto VI, a day acolytes of the franchise say will be bigger than the biggest sporting events.
Details surrounding GTA VI, set in the fictional world of Leonida and its metropolis, the Miami-esque Vice City, have been scarce. But Rockstar Games has been building hype for months, driving supercars along Florida streets, planning a music festival and drip-feeding clips to a ravenous public.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The ‘moon landing’ of gaming: Australians, some of the first to play GTA VI, prepare to descend on Vice City

articles.author: Raphael Rashid in Seoul
articles.description:
South Korea has been gripped by revelations of AI-aided cheating, just days before more than half a million students are to sit high-stakes entrance exams
The integrity of South Korea’s career-defining university entrance exam has been thrown into doubt after the top scorer in a recent professional exam admitted using a concealed camera and AI to cheat.
On Thursday, more than half a million people, mostly school students, are due to sit the exam, known as the suneung, at 1,312 centres across the country. The exam runs for a gruelling eight hours over a single day and determines which university a candidate can attend and, in turn, their future prospects.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: South Korea’s high-stakes university exams upended by AI cheating scandal

articles.author: Reuters
articles.description:
Asif Merchant, allegedly linked to Iran, found by court to have sought retribution over Qassem Suleimani death
A Pakistani man was sentenced to more than 27 years in prison on Tuesday for plotting to assassinate Donald Trump in retaliation for the US killing of Revolutionary Guards commander Qassem Suleimani, the Department of Justice said.
Asif Merchant, who had alleged ties to Iran, sought to hire a hitman to assassinate a politician or a government official in the United States, a Brooklyn court found.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Pakistani man sentenced to 27 years in US prison over Trump murder plot

articles.author: Nadeem Badshah
articles.description:
Lt Col Brandon Carroll Tyner was arrested by British police on 10 November over allegations related to espionage 
A US soldier who was arrested in the UK on suspicion of spying for Russia has been taken into custody by the US military, police have said.
Lt Col Brandon Carroll Tyner, 41, was detained by British counter-terrorism police ‌on 10 November in Gloucestershire over allegations relating ⁠to espionage.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: American soldier held in UK suspected of spying for Russia taken into US military custody

articles.author: Lisa O’Carroll Senior correspondent
articles.description:
CBI says restrictions on cross-Channel work trips are hindering investment and trade between UK and Europe
Business chiefs have called on the UK government and the European Commission to urgently ease Brexit restrictions on business travel for cross-Channel work trips.
A group representing industry bosses said it wants commitments from Andy Burnham and European political leaders that the restrictions will be one of the priorities in 2027 for furthering ties between the two sides, after a summit in Brussels this week.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Brexit work travel rules need urgent improvement, say UK business leaders

articles.author: Lisa O’Carroll and Pippa Crerar
articles.description:
Exclusive: deal expected to be sealed in principle at EU-UK summit on Friday but trickier elements could be postponed for six months
The new post-Brexit UK-EU youth mobility scheme may not come fully into force until 2030.
It will be a disappointment to any under-30s in the UK and the EU who hoped to travel, work or study in each other’s territories from next year after the long-awaited new deal.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: New UK-EU youth mobility scheme may not fully launch until 2030

articles.author: Associated Press in Jerusalem
articles.description:
Knesset’s appointment of Matan Kahana marks step towards reversing policies of outgoing government
The Israeli parliament elected a new speaker on Tuesday, a key step toward rolling back policies passed by the outgoing government led by the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu.
The new speaker is Matan Kahana, an ally of Gadi Eisenkot, the party leader currently working to form the next government and replace Netanyahu.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Israeli parliament elects new speaker backed by Netanyahu’s opponents

articles.author: Natricia Duncan Caribbean correspondent
articles.description:
St Kitts and Nevis to wind down citizenship-by-investment program after EU warns of end to visa-free access
The decision by St Kitts and Nevis to end a lucrative programme offering citizenship to wealthy foreigners in exchange for investment threatens its economy and ability to support people in need, the premier of the island of Nevis has warned.
On Friday, Terrance Drew, the prime minister of the twin-island Caribbean nation, announced he would wind down the citizenship-by-investment (CBI) programme, after the European Union threatened to end visa-free access for St Kitts and Nevis.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Caribbean nations fear economic impact of shuttering citizenship program after EU threats

articles.author: Agence France-Presse
articles.description:
Indigenous Awá people of Amazon make contact with villagers and accept food to take back to territory
About 20 Indigenous people emerged from isolation in Brazil’s Amazon rainforest, several organizations reported on Tuesday, raising the alarm about increased invasions into the tribe’s territory.
According to the NGO Survival International, members of the Awá people, who live in voluntary isolation, arrived on Monday in a village and made contact with a government team in a “historic encounter”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Isolated Brazilian tribe emerges amid alarm over threats to group’s way of life

articles.author: Cecilia Nowell
articles.description:
Child reunited with family after he was detained by immigration agents in San Diego and transferred to Texas
An eight-year-old Haitian boy who was put into restraints and detained by immigration agents in San Diego on 4 November and transferred to a facility in Texas has been reunited with his family in California.
Representative Juan Vargas shared a photograph of the boy and his family in a social media post on Monda, writing: “11 days ago, an 8-year-old in San Diego was taken into federal custody during an immigration check-in. He was separated from his loved ones and held in a facility in Texas. Today, he’s finally home.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Eight-year-old Haitian boy returns home after release from ICE custody

articles.author: Lorenzo Tondo and Sufian Taha in Jerusalem
articles.description:
Bullet hit 72-year-old Fadha Wadha in head outside her home in al-Duyuk al-Tahta, in the West Bank, say residents
A 72-year-old Palestinian woman has been shot dead in an overnight attack by Israeli settlers in a village near Jericho where settlers have recently moved in after taking over several Palestinian homes.
Fadha Wadha was standing outside her home in al-Duyuk al-Tahta in the occupied West Bank when she was struck in the head by a bullet as Israeli settlers fired towards Palestinian houses, according to testimonies from residents. Several other Palestinians, including her son, were wounded by gunfire.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Palestinian woman shot dead by Israeli settlers near Jericho, witnesses say

articles.author: Cris Seda Chabrier
articles.description:
High-stakes hearing comes in wake of resignation from Nvidia after alleged affair with suspected Chinese spy
Nvidia’s former CEO Jensen Huang will testify before several congressional committees on 1 December, setting the stage for a high-stakes hearing in the wake of his resignation following an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
Tim Teter, Nvidia’s general counsel, has also agreed to appear for a closed-door transcribed interview the following day, 2 December.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Jensen Huang to testify before Congress on ‘potential breach of national security’

articles.author: William Christou
articles.description:
Digital monitors recorded 400% rise in posts attacking Arab Israelis, including Netanyahu’s disproven fraud allegations 
Anti-Arab hate speech surged on social media in Israel around the country’s general election last month, digital monitors have said, as politicians including Benjamin Netanyahu levelled disproven allegations against Arab Israeli parties of election fraud.
A new report by the Israel-based Brandeis Institute and FakeReporter recorded a deluge of anti-Arab discourse across social media platforms such as X, Facebook, Instagram and TikTok in the days surrounding Israel’s 27 October election.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Anti-Arab hate speech surged on social media during Israel’s election, report finds

articles.author: Luke Harding in Kyiv
articles.description:
With the SpaceX satellite system faltering, Ukraine’s military launched a surprise, multi-pronged attack to take down vital bridge to Crimea
At 10pm on Monday evening a Ukrainian soldier scrawled a message on a kamikaze drone. It said simply: “The bridge is fucked.” He then added: “We will stand and Moscow will fall.” It was a freezing night, with a bright starry sky and no clouds. Lines of ice had formed on the drone’s bulky wings. Soon, it would be hurtling towards its target – about 500km to the south.
Typically the soldiers who gathered in this muddy field in central Ukraine were attacking oil refineries deep inside Russia. In recent months the work had become almost mundane: they had hit so many of them. The objective that evening, however, was unique. It was a structure personally associated with Vladimir Putin and his grandiose imperial ambitions.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: How Ukraine struck the Kerch bridge, a symbol of Putin’s rule

articles.author: Reuters
articles.description:
Camilo Rodriguez’s death comes as the country grapples with a surge in drug violence 
The Costa Rican journalist Camilo Rodríguez, who gained prominence for publishing allegations against ⁠suspected drug traffickers and politicians, was shot dead on Monday, authorities said.
The first known killing of a journalist ⁠in Costa Rica in ⁠25 years, ​Rodriguez’s death comes as the country grapples with a surge in drug violence driven by international trafficking groups, despite long ⁠being regarded as one of Central America’s most peaceful and stable democracies.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Costa Rican journalist shot dead in first such killing in 25 years

articles.author: Kate Connolly in Berlin
articles.description:
Pop-singing sisters, who died aged 89 last year, described their declining health and desire to depart life together
Alice and Ellen Kessler, the identical pop-singing twins who chose to jointly end their lives through assisted dying last year, said they had “reached rock bottom” due to health problems and had been relieved to be able to die together.
The German sisters, who became huge television stars in the 1960s and 70s, especially in Italy and the US, said a catalogue of health conditions had left them with no desire to carry on living.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Spared a lot’: Kessler twins explained assisted dying decision in final letter

articles.author: Dan Sabbagh Kyiv
articles.description:
Partial demolition of bridge linking Russia and occupied Crimea is obvious embarrassment to Putin days before meeting with Xi and Trump

Europe live – latest updates

Ukraine’s attack on the Kerch road bridge overnight is the culmination of weeks, and perhaps months, of military operations plus years of industrial development, during which Kyiv has developed its own cruise missiles and long-range drones.
The demolition is not quite total, because the rail bridge is still standing, one line in operation – but the attack is an obvious embarrassment to Russia two days before Vladimir Putin is due to meet Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in Shenzhen.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘They were keeping it for a rainy day’: Ukraine’s Kerch bridge attack is proof Kyiv still has cards to play

articles.author: Rachel Leingang
articles.description:
US officials ‘debate whether Iran can or will attempt to execute’ plot to detonate a ‘dirty bomb’, report says
Donald Trump has claimed the US is “looking into” whether Iran is developing plans to detonate a so-called “dirty bomb” in Washington, even as the White House said there were “no credible threats” at this time.
Trump said his administration takes the idea “very seriously”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump claims US is ‘looking into’ Iranian bomb plot in Washington despite ‘no credible threats’

articles.author: Rebecca Bailey in Shenzhen
articles.description:
Host city offers showcase of China’s rise into a confident and innovative power central to global economy
In a Shenzhen square on a balmy evening, locals and tourists watched the dozens of glinting towers that make up the city’s skyline ripple through the colour spectrum – cyan and violet, cyber green, China’s national scarlet and gold – repeatedly flashing the words “Apec 2026”.
The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit is a dream showcase for one of China’s most advanced cities, and the country’s leader, Xi Jinping, is basking in its neon glow.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Hi-tech Shenzhen takes centre stage as Xi sends ‘Chinamaxxing’ message at Apec summit

articles.author: Tom McIlroy in Manila
articles.description:
Organisers say up to 10,000 people could join next round of demonstrations as US president arrives for Asean summit

Asean and Apec summits – as it happened

Hundreds of people have been arrested in heated demonstrations against Donald Trump in Manila, as the US president arrived in the city for a leaders’ summit.
Organisers claimed as many as 10,000 people would be joining protests against Trump in the capital of the Philippines on Tuesday, where he is attending the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit. The crowds were expected to try to march to the summit site.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Hundreds arrested in anti-Trump protests in Philippines amid anger over Iran war and AI pact

articles.author: Niha Masih
articles.description:
As tourism booms, three experienced female travellers give their take on how to make the most of travelling here
• Don’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up here
The 13th-century Persian scholar Zakariyya al-Qazwini never travelled to India. But he catalogued it in his famous work The Wonders of Creation and Rarities of Existence, which drew on accounts of a distant land filled with “rarities par excellence”. For al-Qazwini, as Helen Pfeifer writes in the London Review of Books, wonder was not an emotion but an intellectual method of making sense of the world and acquiring knowledge.
India has long occupied such a space in the global imagination, as a land of extraordinary riches; spirituality, customs, chaos and contradictions. This has shaped how the country is perceived from afar, but it can often flatten its complexities.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: India has been named a ‘destination of the year’ for 2027 – here are insiders’ tips on travelling beyond the tropes

articles.author: Matthew Pearce
articles.description:
About a third of cases involved chemicals banned for use on EU farms, according to investigation by Unearthed and Public Eye 
Pesticides sold by European chemical companies were named in more than 1,600 poisoning reports in Brazil last year, an investigation has found.
About a third of the cases involved chemicals banned from use on farms in the EU because of the risks they pose to people and the environment. But European companies are not banned from manufacturing these chemicals, as long as they export them overseas to countries where they are legally allowed to be used.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: European-made pesticides named in 1,605 poisoning reports in Brazil last year

articles.author: Jennifer Rankin in Brussels
articles.description:
Germany, Austria, Netherlands, Denmark and Greece likely to face challenges to policy criticised as ‘grave moral failing’
Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”.
The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Five EU states announce plans for immigration ‘return hubs’ in Rwanda

articles.author: Guardian sport
articles.description:
Suspect named as Greene Da’monte Khiree

Drug smuggling carries life sentence in Nigeria

An American basketball player has been arrested in Nigeria for allegedly attempting to smuggle 33.95kg (75lb) of marijuana into the country.
Nigeria’s National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) said a 28-year-old player named as Greene Da’monte Khiree from the state of Georgia was arrested at Lagos’s main airport last Wednesday after he arrived on a flight from Thailand via the United Arab Emirates.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: US basketball player arrested with 75lb of marijuana at Nigerian airport, say authorities

articles.author: Imran Lodhi, as told to Morgan Krakow
articles.description:
When the floods hit Pakistan he went out to help. Then the water reached his own family. This is Imran Lodhi’s story
Location: Dera Ghazi Khan, Pakistan
Disaster: Pakistan intense monsoon rainfall
Imran Lodhi is a university lecturer with a doctorate in climate change and sustainable development. The 41-year-old was living in Dera Ghazi Khan, a city in south-western Punjab, when floods devastated provinces across Pakistan. Climate change made the monsoon rainfall that caused the floods more intense.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘I saw a picture of a two-year-old girl buried in mud. I knew we had to do something’ – This is climate breakdown

articles.author: Rachel Savage in Johannesburg
articles.description:
Demonstrators tried to block vehicle carrying the baboons, whose capture authorities say is needed to protect both primate and human
The relocation of a troop of baboons in Cape Town to a wildlife sanctuary has triggered furious protests by local people opposed to their capture, which officials argue is necessary to stop human-wildlife conflict in the city.
The 44-member Waterfall troop (named after the area they mainly inhabit) was captured in the southern seaside suburb of Simon’s Town on Friday and Saturday. A second, smaller Seaforth troop is also due to be moved.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Relocation of Cape Town baboons to sanctuary ignites heated protests

articles.author: Oliver Holmes and Kaamil Ahmed
articles.description:
International court of justice has never before found a state guilty of genocide, and ruling will have implications for case against Israel
The world’s top court will deliver a judgment this week on whether Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, in a landmark case that will set a critical 21st-century benchmark for the gravest of all international crimes.
The closely watched judgment could become one of the most significant moments in international law since the end of the second world war.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: World’s top court to rule if Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya

articles.author: Rachel Savage in Johannesburg and agencies
articles.description:
After a month-long investigation it was concluded that Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which won the £10,000 Caine prize, was ‘human-written’
The Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza has been cleared of using AI to write a prize-winning short story, after the prestigious Caine prize for African writers concluded that his entry was “human-written” after a month-long investigation.
Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which charts the declining fortunes of a family after the father invests in fish tanks, was announced as the winner of the £10,000 prize on 6 October.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza cleared of using AI to write prize-winning story

articles.author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen and Aakash Hassan in Delhi
articles.description:
Former prime minister faces death penalty upon return after being sentenced in absentia over deaths in 2024 uprising
Sheikh Hasina is “confident” she will return to Bangladesh in December, according to exiled members of her party, after the disgraced former prime minister applied for a new passport this week.
Hasina has been living in self-imposed exile since August 2024 when she was toppled from power by a mass uprising against her authoritarian rule. She crossed the border to India, where she has since been allowed to live freely in Delhi.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Disgraced former leader Sheikh Hasina plans return to Bangladesh from exile

articles.author: Niha Masih
articles.description:
From the assassinations of her husband and mother-in-law to press stonewalling under Modi, Belonging offers an insider’s account of India’s political evolution
• Don’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up here
Few love stories have been as closely entwined with a nation’s history as that of Sonia and Rajiv Gandhi. The former’s much-awaited political memoir, Belonging, offers a strikingly candid account of her journey from a small town in Italy to the highest echelons of power in India – all for love, she says.
The veteran Congress party leader has been fiercely protective of her personal world. In Belonging, she opens up for the first time about the extraordinary twists and turns of a life that has largely unfolded in full public view. (The Guardian’s Hannah Ellis-Petersen has a rare in-person interview with Gandhi, and you can read an excerpt from the book here.)
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Grenades, grief and a deepening political divide: five takeaways from Sonia Gandhi’s new memoir

articles.author: Ed Pilkington in Anchorage, Alaska
articles.description:
Peltola, the first Alaska Native in the US Senate, ran a campaign that drew universal issues from her own Indigenous politics
Late into the night on 3 November, while the lower 48 states were reeling from the blue wave crashing across the US, Mary Peltola took to the stage in a Sheraton Hotel ballroom in Anchorage, Alaska, to greet her supporters.
It wasn’t a victory speech as such – there would still be long days ahead before all votes could be counted across this vast arctic state. But that didn’t prevent the Democratic Senate candidate from expressing her elation, bouncing up and down on stage, clapping her hands and clicking her fingers.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Aarigaa!’: the triumph of Mary Peltola’s historic US Senate win and what it means for Alaska Natives

articles.author: Chris Stein
articles.description:
Republican incumbent beaten in race dominated by controversy over second candidate named Dan Sullivan
Democrat Mary Peltola will be Alaska’s next senator after beating the Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan, with the result called two weeks on from midterm elections which saw Donald Trump’s party lose ground across the country.
Peltola, a former US House lawmaker, is the first Democrat the state has elected to the Senate since 2008. Her victory comes just two years after Alaska voters unseated her while supporting Trump by a double-digit margin.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Mary Peltola beats Republican Dan Sullivan in Alaska to give Democrats 56 Senate seats

articles.author: Cecilia Nowell, Shrai Popat, Lucy Campbell and Tom Ambrose
articles.description:
This live blog is now closed.

White House withdraws nomination of Heidi Overton to lead FDA

Sign up for US Breaking News email

Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic-Senator elect from Michigan, said today that he would be happy to work with the Trump administration to pass one of his tentpole policy agenda items – Medicare For All.
“Everybody’s like, ‘ah well, you’d work with Donald Trump to get Medicare For All?’. I’m like hell yeah, because the point for me is Medicare For All. I don’t care who puts their name on it. I need to go back and talk to Michiganders, and I need to know that our service made their lives easier,” he said at the Atlantic Summit in Washington DC.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: White House pulls nomination of Heidi Overton to lead Food and Drug Administration – as it happened

articles.author: Cecilia Nowell
articles.description:
Move to drop Trump ally and prominent abortion opponent comes a day before key Senate health committee vote
The White House has dropped its nomination of Heidi Overton to lead the Food and Drug Administration, a White House official told the Guardian.
Donald Trump nominated Overton – a physician and prominent abortion opponent – in August. Overton has spent most of her professional career working directly for Trump or conservative groups aligned with his agenda. Her nomination in August was seen as a move to bring a stabilizing Trump loyalist to the agency after a tumultous year under Trump’s first FDA commissioner, Marty Makary.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: White House withdraws nomination of Heidi Overton to lead FDA

articles.author: Reuters
articles.description:
Asif Merchant, allegedly linked to Iran, found by court to have sought retribution over Qassem Suleimani death
A Pakistani man was sentenced to more than 27 years in prison on Tuesday for plotting to assassinate Donald Trump in retaliation for the US killing of Revolutionary Guards commander Qassem Suleimani, the Department of Justice said.
Asif Merchant, who had alleged ties to Iran, sought to hire a hitman to assassinate a politician or a government official in the United States, a Brooklyn court found.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Pakistani man sentenced to 27 years in US prison over Trump murder plot

articles.description:
Hung Cao, the acting US navy secretary, who faced lawmakers to be confirmed as the permanent top official, said during his confirmation hearing that the eight suicide attempts on board the USS Abraham Lincoln – which returned last month from a record-breaking deployment rife with mental health crises and concerns about living conditions – were actually “suicide mitigations”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Acting US navy secretary refers to eight suicide attempts as 'suicide mitigations' – video

articles.author: Arwa Mahdawi
articles.description:
Now the vice-president’s luck is turning, he seems reluctant to commit himself to the next presidential race – and I, for one, hate to see it
How do you think history will remember JD Vance? As the first vice-president to spark a vigorous debate about their eyeliner routine? As one of the last public figures to see Pope Francis alive? As the only politician in US history to have been the subject of a rumour about sexual relations with a couch (even though it was unfounded)?
I have no idea. But it seems increasingly unlikely he will be remembered as the 48th president of the US. After Maga’s midterm thrashing, Vance’s political future doesn’t look as bright as it used to. So much so that there has been a flurry of recent headlines debating whether or not Vance, once considered Donald Trump’s heir apparent, may slink away from a presidential run altogether.
Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in our letters section, please click here.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Should JD Vance run for president? I say go for it, habibi! | Arwa Mahdawi

articles.author: Gabrielle Canon in Antalya
articles.description:
The 120-strong America Is All In group are trying to ensure that the US won’t remained sidelined at the climate talks for very much longer. Plus: wild oysters are back in Scotland and a super El Niño looms over Cop
• Don’t get Down to Earth delivered to your inbox? Sign up here
The final week of Cop31 is in full swing, with just four days left to set a broad range of climate commitments into concrete action. I am on the ground at this year’s UN annual climate summit, where thousands of world leaders, businesses, nonprofits and scientists have converged in Antalya, Turkey, and there’s a lot left to do as the clock ticks down.
“Nearly 200 countries are working through 165 mandates,” executive secretary Simon Stiell told reporters at the midpoint on Saturday, pushing for a swift move to the hardest issues and championing compromise. “Each country has a view,” he said. “Every country has a voice.”
European-made pesticides named in 1,605 poisoning reports in Brazil last year
AI models ‘weak and fallible’ on climate science, UN-backed study reports
‘I was home alone when the glacier collapsed. My mum called and told me to run’
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘We are all in’: the Democrats trying to turn round the US’s reputation at Cop31

articles.author: Wajahat Ali
articles.description:
America’s future depends on progressive, anti-establishment fighters
Welcome back to How We Win, a Guardian opinion series with leading thinkers, offering bold ideas for America’s political future. Last week, Naomi Klein, Guardian US columnist, argued for taking on the billionaire class. Today’s edition was written by Wajahat Ali, editor of The Left Hook and co-host of The Democracy-ish Podcast.
Change is slow, and then, once in a while, all of a sudden.
The future of America depends on progressive, anti-establishment fighters to champion a politics of transformation.
Tax billionaires.
Medicare for All.
Abolish ICE and put forth an immigration reform policy that centers both humanity and security.
Call out Israel’s genocide and withhold money and weapons from foreign countries that commit war crimes with our resources.
A living wage.
Reject corporate Pac money and deliver campaign finance reform.
Combat climate change and move away from fossil fuels.
Expand and aggressively reform the supreme court, because without that, we get nothing.
Deliver accountability for “the Epstein class”, a transnational syndicate of powerful billionaires who commit crimes with impunity.
Never sacrifice or abandon any marginalized group in our pursuit of affordability and accountability.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Let’s take over the ossified Democratic party and deliver a modern New Deal

articles.author: Anna North
articles.description:
From Utah to Louisiana, US states are making menopause care more affordable and accessible for midlife women
Melissa Shusterman was desperate for help with her menopausal symptoms: body aches, lethargy and brain fog, which she described as feeling “not myself”. The Pennsylvania state representative saw a gynecologist, a physical therapist, a chiropractor and a urologist. One doctor gave her lubricant, even though she’d already explained to him that sex was not the problem. (“Have you seen my husband?” she quipped.)
“I am more than lubrication,” Shusterman said. “I am a dynamic, smart, hardworking woman who wants to continue to feel good, so I can join my contemporaries, get back to work, and change things.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Menopause symptoms aren’t always taken seriously. These female lawmakers plan to change that

articles.author: Sidney Blumenthal
articles.description:
Horowitz, who swung from the far left to the far right, sought total political warfare against institutions and immigration 
Stephen Miller has risen to the top of the White House in the downdraft of Donald Trump’s abject defeat in the midterm elections. It is no irony to Trump that he has elevated Miller as his ideal bullying enforcer only after Trump’s own thorough repudiation. Appointing Miller is Trump’s denial that he is the worst thing he could possibly imagine: a loser.
Trump has no more time for adults in the room who might want to negotiate with the new powers-that-be in the Congress. He has searched his soul, as he explained in his interview on 60 Minutes, entertaining his wish to ascend to heaven.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: How the rightwing operative David Horowitz shaped Stephen Miller | Sidney Blumenthal

articles.author: Becca Andrews
articles.description:
Charismatic worship, which promises ‘deliverance’ from evil, has taken hold across Christian churches, the right and on social media
Slumped on the ground, the young woman pressed her forehead against the warm pavement of a twilit parking lot in Columbia, Tennessee.
Two other women dressed in white T-shirts identifying them as members of the ministry attended to her, praying over her prone body, speaking to her in low, urgent tones. Her whimpers escalated into moans and then crescendoed into guttural cries: “No! No! No!”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘I know I sound crazy’: the creep of demons into American evangelical churches

articles.author: Hosted by Kai Wright with Chris Stein and Rachel Leingang, produced by Monica Espitia and Anabel Bacon, engineered by Ivan Kuraev , executive producer Rachel Humphreys
articles.description:
The blue wave has hit Washington, and with the flood of new Democratic lawmakers comes a debate over who should lead the party. On Monday, Maryland senator Chris Van Hollen said his campaign to unseat Chuck Schumer as Senate majority leader is gathering momentum. He has painted himself as the underdog candidate to Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats for nearly a decade. What does this leadership battle tell us about the kind of party Democrats want to be? Kai Wright speaks to the Guardian’s senior politics reporter Chris Stein about Van Hollen's chances, and hears from the Guardian's midwest political correspondent Rachel Leingang about why new senators in her region are having doubts about Schumer
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Can Chris Van Hollen really beat Chuck Schumer? – Stateside with Kai and Carter

articles.author: Guthrie Scrimgeour
articles.description:
During the midterm elections, Ni‘ihau backed Democrats for their governors, casting 14 of their 21 votes for Josh Green and Derek Kawakami
The secluded island of Ni‘ihau has long been a Republican stronghold in deep blue Hawai‘i. Ni‘ihauans have an unusual tendency to unanimously support conservative candidates, like in 2020, when all 43 Ni‘ihauan voters cast their ballots for Donald Trump.
This has been the case since as far back as the early 1900s, when Ni‘ihau’s ballots were sometimes relayed to the neighboring island of Kaua‘i via carrier pigeon. The headline of one characteristic 1939 Honolulu Star Bulletin article reads – “Ni‘ihau Casts 59 Votes All For GOP as Usual.” Bush beat Kerry 39-0, Reagan beat Carter 56-1, and Nixon beat Kennedy 99-0.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Even Hawaiʻi’s most Republican island can’t escape the blue wave

articles.author: Robert Reich
articles.description:
The party’s big-tent approach has caused post-election feuding in the past. But a pair of singular goals can prevent it
Democrats usually suffer big tent disease. To win, they put together such large coalitions of voters – working class, middle class, Black people, Latinos, women, young people, moderates, liberals – that once they’re in office, intraparty feuds often threaten their agenda.
Will it happen again when they take power in January? I don’t think so. Two outside forces will keep Democrats glued together.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Two reasons Democrats can overcome infighting next year | Robert Reich

articles.author: Presented by Lucy Hough with Aisha Down ; produced by Hana Williams ; senior producer Angus Neale ; executive producer Zoe Hitch
articles.description:
Jensen Huang’s resignation from the AI chipmaker Nvidia has sent shockwaves through the global economy. Huang resigned after reported affairs with an Nvidia executive and a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy. The fallout is not over yet, with criticism mounting over the apparent lack of action from the US commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick. Lucy Hough speaks to the Guardian’s global technology reporter, Aisha Down
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Why the Nvidia scandal is far from over - The Latest

articles.author: Presented by Jonathan Freedland , with Susan Glasser, produced by Danielle Stephens and May Robson
articles.description:
Jonathan Freedland speaks to Susan Glasser of the New Yorker about why Trump’s judgment of high-profile men is questionable
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Why the Nvidia cheating scandal is bad for Trump | Politics Weekly America

articles.author: Andrew Gregory Health editor
articles.description:
Campaign groups and regulators say data breaches are distressing for patients and families and erode trust in the health service
The NHS in England has recorded more than 3,000 incidents of staff inappropriately snooping on patients’ medical records in the last five years.
Patient campaign groups and regulators said the figures were “deeply concerning” and distressing for patients and families, and eroded trust in the health service. A lack of transparency from NHS organisations after data breaches were uncovered further compounded the heartache, they added.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Deeply concerning’: NHS in England reports more than 3,000 incidents of staff snooping on patients’ records

articles.author: Neha Gohil Midlands correspondent
articles.description:
Party promised a Musk-inspired blitz at councils in England, but research shows it has failed to cut harder or faster than comparable local authorities
When Reform UK secured a historic breakthrough in the May local elections last year, it was – according to the party leader, Nigel Farage – time for the UK to emulate Donald Trump and make sweeping local government cuts.
At the time, the US president had enlisted the world’s richest man, Elon Musk, to run his “department of government efficiency” (Doge). During a 16-week blitz at the heart of the US government, Musk caused chaos, fired tens of thousands of workers and gutted USAID.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘In the end, nothing happened’: how Reform’s Doge-style crackdown fell flat

articles.author: Robyn Vinter North of England correspondent
articles.description:
Lasting cross-class friendships involve routinely ‘taking the piss’ out of the more privileged party, research by the LSE shows
Routinely “taking the piss” out of more privileged friends is one of the main ways people cope with a class difference in their friendships, research has found.
Cross-class friendships are widespread and mutually beneficial, a study by the London School of Economics showed, but a class gap can still pose an “omnipresent threat” to friendships.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: How to deal with a class difference in friendships? Make fun of your privileged friends

articles.author: Dan Milmo Global technology editor
articles.description:
Meaning and use of word has become more important in age of AI chatbot, says dictionary
In a world where the line between people and machines is more blurred than ever, Cambridge dictionary has sided with natural intelligence for its word of the year: human.
Breakthroughs in artificial intelligence – led by the arrival of ChatGPT three years ago – have made the question of what it means to be human as vexed as ever, but the dictionary has drawn a firm line with its choice of the word of 2026, defining “human” as “having the qualities, faults, and feelings that people have, as opposed to gods, animals, or machines”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Human’ wins Cambridge dictionary’s word of the year

articles.author: Hanad Ahmed
articles.description:
Research also shows consuming wine could cut risk, reopening debate on whether beverage has health benefits
Drinking beer and spirits increases the risk of serious kidney damage, whereas consuming wine offers protection against it, a study suggests.
People who drink nine units of spirits a week are 26% more likely to suffer acute kidney injury than those who consume only one unit a week.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Drinking beer and spirits raises risk of acute kidney damage, study suggests

articles.author: Presented by Nosheen Iqbal; produced by George McDonagh, Ivor Manley , Harriet Mogie and Rudi Zygadlo; executive producer Eli Block
articles.description:
There are about a million young people across the country not in employment, education or training. Could Alan Milburn’s landmark report help change that? Richard Partington reports
The UK has one of the worst rates in Europe when it comes to youth unemployment. From the savage cuts to youth services during austerity, to the impacts of the pandemic and now the threat of AI to entry level jobs, young people across the country are feeling that the social contract is broken.
But now Alan Milburn, the 68-year-old New Labour veteran, has published a radical review urging the government to spend billions on a new deal for young people.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Can Labour end the youth unemployment crisis? – podcast

articles.author: Nadeem Badshah
articles.description:
Lt Col Brandon Carroll Tyner was arrested by British police on 10 November over allegations related to espionage 
A US soldier who was arrested in the UK on suspicion of spying for Russia has been taken into custody by the US military, police have said.
Lt Col Brandon Carroll Tyner, 41, was detained by British counter-terrorism police ‌on 10 November in Gloucestershire over allegations relating ⁠to espionage.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: American soldier held in UK suspected of spying for Russia taken into US military custody

articles.author: Vikram Dodd Police and crime correspondent
articles.description:
After damning report into standards at the top of forces in England and Wales, 200 people a year with superintendent potential to be recruited
Hundreds of people will be trained to boost “frankly inadequate” leadership of law enforcement, the home secretary is to say.
Shabana Mahmood will tell police chiefs and leaders at their central London annual conference on Wednesday that standards must improve as she unveils a scheme to train 200 people a year, after a report in June into police leadership found it was at times “staggeringly” poor.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Shabana Mahmood to launch fast-track training to improve police leadership

articles.author: Jasper Jolly, Jillian Ambrose and Kiran Stacey
articles.description:
Analysts say mooted move to let more petrol and diesel vehicles be sold would wreck plan to reach net zero by 2050

Weakening the UK’s electric car sales rules would probably cause the government to miss legally binding climate targets, according to advisers tracking Britain’s progress to net zero.
The analysis by the Climate Change Committee (CCC) suggests the policy would blow a hole in the plan for achieving net zero carbon emissions by 2050 – prompting concerns that Andy Burnham’s government will have to slash the UK’s carbon emissions reduction targets, known as the carbon budgets.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK will miss climate targets if it weakens EV sales rules, advisers warn

articles.author: Lisa O’Carroll Senior correspondent
articles.description:
CBI says restrictions on cross-Channel work trips are hindering investment and trade between UK and Europe
Business chiefs have called on the UK government and the European Commission to urgently ease Brexit restrictions on business travel for cross-Channel work trips.
A group representing industry bosses said it wants commitments from Andy Burnham and European political leaders that the restrictions will be one of the priorities in 2027 for furthering ties between the two sides, after a summit in Brussels this week.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Brexit work travel rules need urgent improvement, say UK business leaders

articles.author: Richard Adams Education editor
articles.description:
England’s exam regulator says those caught using AI or smart glasses face disqualification from GCSEs and A-levels
Students in England could suffer “life-altering” penalties if they are caught relying on AI or smart glasses to cheat, England’s qualifications regulator has said.
The head of Ofqual, Ian Bauckham, said students could be disqualified from GCSEs, A-levels and other qualifications if they tried to use AI in assessed coursework, and called for retailers to be barred from marketing wearable technology for exam cheating.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Ofqual urges ‘life-altering’ penalties for students who use tech to cheat

articles.author: Sally Weale Education correspondent
articles.description:
Vice-chancellor halts proposed relocation from Stratford-upon-Avon but offers no guarantees over future
The University of Birmingham has paused plans to move its much-loved Shakespeare Institute from Stratford-upon-Avon to its city campus after an outcry from scholars, actors and enthusiasts around the world.
Prof Adam Tickell, the university’s vice-chancellor and principal, issued a statement on Tuesday evening saying proposals to relocate the institute and its renowned 60,000-volume library to the university’s Edgbaston campus would be put on hold while its future was explored.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: University of Birmingham pauses plans to move Shakespeare Institute after outcry

articles.author: Patrick Butler Social policy editor
articles.description:
He lays out sweeping aims and finer details for how to fix the Neets crisis – and is obsessive about welfare

Neet ideas: what’s in Milburn’s report?

It is not clear if too many people were expecting Everything Everywhere All at Once, but that is what Alan Milburn has delivered. From a Welfare State to a Working State is almost absurdly ambitious. The terms of reference said something about the drivers of youth labour markets. We got a blueprint for how to fix everything and everyone.
What Keir Starmer, who commissioned it, had in mind, we’ll never know, but Milburn has taken up with gusto Andy Burnham’s general invocation to think boldly and rewire the state. Yes, it’s about training and jobs, but it’s also about pulling apart the NHS, giving schools and colleges an MOT, and once again, blowing up old-fashioned social security.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Milburn’s absurdly ambitious report offers blueprint for fixing everything and everyone

articles.author: Kiran Stacey and Richard Partington
articles.description:
Youth unemployment review risks clash with unions and Labour left over workers’ rights and minimum wage

Neet ideas: what’s in Alan Milburn’s youth unemployment report?

Who are the Neets? UK youth job crisis in five charts

Milburn urges Burnham to spend billions on young people

Alan Milburn has called on ministers to cut business taxes and ease regulations to encourage employers to hire more young people, setting up a potential clash with trade unions and the Labour left over employment rights.
The former health secretary published the results of his year-long review into youth unemployment on Wednesday, in what the prime minister, Andy Burnham, called a “watershed moment” for young people.

articles.title: Milburn calls for tax cuts for businesses hiring young people despite union concerns

This chart, from the Milburn report, shows what is likely to happen to the Neet rate, with or without the Milburn policies.
The Alan Milburn report has now formally been published. It should be online here very soon.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Burnham delays announcement about options for closer relationship with EU until next month – as it happened

articles.author: Jonathan Watts
articles.description:
We look at what is happening over the Arctic and what it might mean for winter weather in the northern hemisphere
The polar vortex has flipped direction, signalling the earliest “major sudden stratospheric warming” ever observed. We examine how it is likely to affect you and whether it will bring snow.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: What is the polar vortex, why has it flipped and will it bring the UK snow?

articles.author: Jessica Murray  and Neha Gohil
articles.description:
Labour’s plan to get young unemployed people into work involves overhaul of welfare support, but for those with disabilities, specialist help is crucial
When Rory Bowman finished school he joined the cohort of almost a million Neets – young people not in education, employment or training – around the country.
The 21-year-old has autism and said he was exhausted after struggling for support in mainstream education for years. He didn’t think he could manage university, but couldn’t find a job or training that would accommodate his neurodivergence.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘They learn the job doing the job’: the project helping UK’s Neets into work

articles.author: Kiran Stacey and Richard Partington
articles.description:
Government promises spending cuts to pay for the proposals, described by prime minister as ‘watershed moment’

Neet ideas: what’s in Milburn’s report?

Ministers have promised to create an entirely new welfare system for young people as they gave their backing to Alan Milburn’s 278-page report, promising spending cuts next year to help pay for his proposals and giving him a government role to push them through.
Andy Burnham, the prime minister, told his cabinet colleagues on Tuesday morning the report was a “watershed moment” and offered a “comprehensive vision” as he invited its author to address the meeting.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Ministers vow to create new welfare system for young people as they back Milburn report

articles.author: Julia Kollewe
articles.description:
Retailer’s British boss says John Healey ‘missed opportunity to back retailers’ in October’s budget
Ikea has ditched some planned store openings in the UK blaming the cost of business taxes, which it said were the highest in Europe.
As its annual UK sales little more than flatlined at the Swedish flatpack furniture retailer, its UK boss, David McCabe, said: “There are locations where we were planning to open a new unit, and those plans have been abandoned due to the cost that we experience and the complexity within the market.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Ikea ditches plans for new UK stores, blaming high business taxes

Alan Milburn has warned that the UK is at risk of losing a generation of young people without radical reform to tackle youth unemployment. Speaking at the launch of his report at Google's London headquarters, the former health secretary insisted 'half measures will not do' as he outlined proposals to get more young people into work that could save the government £200m a year


Alan Milburn says his plan to get young people into work will save only £200m a year

articles.title: Alan Milburn says 'Great British promise' to young people is being broken – video

articles.author: Phillip Inman
articles.description:
Wage growth falls to 3.5% in September, as ministers examine how best to get young people into work

Milburn urges Burnham to spend billions on young people

Who are the Neets? UK youth job crisis in five charts

The UK unemployment rate has unexpectedly fallen as the government released an important report on the youth jobs crisis.
The unemployment rate was 4.6% in September, dipping from 4.7% in August and down from 5% earlier in the year, according to the Office for National Statistics.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK unemployment unexpectedly eases to 4.6% as government releases Milburn report

articles.author: Joanna Partridge
articles.description:
News of Spanish-owned lender’s policy emerges as other banks are toughening their stance on working from home
Staff at the high street bank Santander have been permitted to log holiday and sick leave as days worked in the office, helping them to meet workplace attendance requirements.
Back-office staff at the Spanish-owned lender have been expected to spend at least 12 working days each month in what the company calls a “head office location”, although this does not apply to staff working in bank branches.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Santander allows staff to count holidays and sick leave as days worked in office

articles.author: Hilary Osborne
articles.description:
Stock market debut of Claude AI chatbot maker is expected to be one of the biggest flotations in history
The technology company Anthropic is heading for a blockbuster stock market listing this week in what is slated to be one of the largest debuts in history.
The company is a leader in artificial intelligence, and is best known for its chatbot Claude. The float, which is expected to value the business at $1.4tn (£1tn), comes at a volatile time for tech stocks, yet it has been reported that the shares could be six times oversubscribed.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Anthropic IPO: how can I buy shares, and is it worth it?

articles.author: Peter Walker Senior political correspondent
articles.description:
Former minister’s 278-page report calls for changes to employment regulations, education, healthcare and benefits

Who are the Neets? UK youth job crisis in five charts

Milburn urges Burnham to spend billions on young people


Five months on from a first report detailing the growing crisis of young people who are not in education, employment or training (Neet), Alan Milburn has produced his recommendations on how to tackle it. Set out over 278 pages, they amount to, as he readily accepts, a major rethink of everything from employment regulations to education, healthcare and benefits.
Here is what he has said.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Neet ideas: what’s in Alan Milburn’s report on young people not in education, employment or training?

articles.author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
articles.description:
Major tours by the likes of Oasis helped make 2025 a lucrative year, with music export revenue reaching £4.8bn
Major tours by Oasis, Robbie Williams and Dua Lipa, as well as hit albums by the likes of Olivia Dean, have helped to push the UK music industry to record revenues.
But there are concerns over a widening gulf in income between A-listers such as these, and the less well-known artists that form the bulk of the UK’s music community.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK music industry hits record high of £8.4bn – but are working musicians being left behind?

About a third of cases involved chemicals banned for use on EU farms, according to investigation by Unearthed and Public Eye

About a third of the cases involved chemicals banned from use on farms in the EU because of the risks they pose to people and the environment. But European companies are not banned from manufacturing these chemicals, as long as they export them overseas to countries where they are legally allowed to be used.

DHSC to extend US tech firm’s contract for two more years to allow time to line up British companies to replace it

The Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) has decided to extend Palantir’s contract to provide the federated data platform (FDP) – the software that links different healthcare providers – for two more years rather than exercise a break clause that would have let them axe it next spring.

Walliams, 55, has been accused of using his power and celebrity status to prey on young women and teenagers for sex, a joint investigation by the Guardian and ITV News has found.

Other international helplines are available for people affected by sexual abuse, childhood abuse, and people in crisis.

Popular edible golden oyster classed as high-risk invasive species because of negative impact on woodlands

Supplies are low and reserves of certain types are half of what the UK needs, officials say
UK blood services have issued an urgent appeal for 150,000 donations to help the NHS cope with the increase in demand that occurs during the winter.

Exclusive: Experts say watering down ZEV mandate would slow market and hamper efforts to reduce cost of living
Moves to weaken the UK’s targets on electric vehicles would hurt the car industry as well as consumers, campaigners and experts have said before a key intervention from government advisers expected this week.
The climate change committee (CCC) will write to ministers on Wednesday about the effects of changing the zero emissions vehicle (ZEV) mandate on the cost of living and the UK’s net zero targets.

Residents of Astley in Greater Manchester will tell public inquiry next week of ‘cacophony’ of noise causing sleep deprivation and depression
When Stephen Retford retired from the police in 2006, he looked forward to a quiet life after nearly three decades catching villains. But now the former detective has landed another big case – one that is extremely close to home.
“It’s the total injustice of it,” the 70-year-old seethed, staring up at the 18-metre-high mega-warehouse that looms over the quiet village of Astley in Greater Manchester. Residents are up in arms about the “monster” construction, likening it to having a “cruise ship in our back garden”.

articles.description:
Scheme in Derry aims to sow confidence by getting people with learning and physical disabilities into wrestling
The music thumped, the lights blazed and from the ring the announcer did a countdown. “Who is ready to rumble?” he roared. The bellows and cheers indicated that the crowd at St Columb’s Hall in Derry on Saturday night was more than ready for the Foyle Rumble, and so began a wrestling extravaganza of heroes and villains in leotards, masks and kneepads.
The blend of athleticism and scripted storytelling would have been familiar to fans of WrestleMania, but this Northern Irish version came with a twist: many of the performers have learning or physical disabilities, and the characters they play in the ring do not quite stay in the ring.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘No matter what, he doesn’t quit’: disabled wrestlers draw strength from ring alter egos

England’s exam regulator says those caught using AI or smart glasses face disqualification from GCSEs and A-levels
Students in England could suffer “life-altering” penalties if they are caught relying on AI or smart glasses to cheat, England’s qualifications regulator has said.

Nvidia announced the same day that its quarterly revenue beat expectations, coming in at $115.84bn, doubling from the same time period a year ago. articles.description:

“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote in a statement published in the Wall Street Journal and CNBC.
Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I’ve never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me.
I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. NVIDIA has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible. I love our country, and I love NVIDIA.

articles.author: Lewis Gordon
articles.description:
PC; Forward Instinct
This irreverent stealth game depicts Samuel’s lonely life robbing garish, midwestern abodes – it’s a Shameless way to make a living
For many people, McMansions are an eyesore, but for the protagonist of Keepsake County, a renowned burglar, they are an enticing opportunity. Prowling at purple-hued dusk, this unfussy thief is just as likely to steal a half-eaten slice of pizza or a naff ceramic ornament as he is an expensive set of golf clubs. It’s a sad, desperate way to make a living, a sense compounded by what this fledgling kleptomaniac carries his loot away in: a plastic shopping bag.
Countless works have taken us to breadline America, from classic novel East of Eden to acclaimed TV crime drama Mare of Easttown. But Keepsake County is no prestige examination of the economic underbelly of the US. Rather, it is a stealing simulator with eccentric Adult Swim-style art and a darkly absurdist sense of humour that is expressed in its moment-to-moment action. For example, when I set off the alarm at a glinting modernist abode, I had to quickly dodge the gunshot fired my way by its maniacal owner, and as I scarpered across the surrounding grassy verge, I grabbed underpants off the clothesline just to make the long drive through the night worth it. I was reminded of Shameless (the US version) as much as Steinbeck.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Keepsake County review – eccentric stealing simulator with a social conscience

Tech on its last legs? Refurbished can be the cheaper, greener option. Here’s how to choose well and avoid the pitfalls
• How to make your phone last longer

What they won’t be so keen to highlight is the huge environmental cost that comes from feeding the capitalist beast year on year, given what an obvious sales vibe-killer it would be.
While the best approach for the planet is to opt out completely and observe the alternative holiday of Buy Nothing Day instead, such an approach can prove self-defeating for your finances in the long term. If you shop smart on Black Friday and avoid the lure of impulse buys, it’s a good time to stock up on the things you need at lower prices than the rest of the year.

articles.author: Lewis Gordon
articles.description:
Featuring hundreds of songs from the hippest real-world artists, the radio stations in Rockstar’s crime sagas are as hotly anticipated as the storylines. Contributors including Flying Lotus, Wavves and Nite Jewel reflect on the soundtracks’ curation and impact
• The exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI
• Crime pays: how GTA became a cultural colossus
• Ten movies (and one TV show) that inspired GTA
A droptop sports car speeds along a highway blaring 90s west coast rap from its booming sound system. Gradually, the asphalt gives way to rural backwaters, and so the sounds of Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas’s local radio also change: less gangster rap and more twangin’ country – the grizzled croon of Merle Haggard and yearning warble of Patsy Cline.
The Grand Theft Auto games are massive, stretching across many, many square miles of virtual terrain. Their soundtracks, relayed mostly via in-game radio stations, are manifold. And these two aspects, plus the personal experiences each player brings to the game, mean everyone has a different favourite musical memory from the smash-hit crime series. For acclaimed electronic musician Flying Lotus, it is all the hours he spent cavorting around 2004’s San Andreas that remain special. “It felt like the first time a game saw a different side of culture – black culture,” he says over the phone. “It felt like we were being seen. And with the extent of the music, all the cool California hip-hop, it felt like someone actually cared.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Killer tunes: how Grand Theft Auto conquered the music world
